Common discrete distributions

Common discrete distributions: topics

  • The standard discrete families: Bernoulli, geometric, binomial, negative binomial, Poisson
    • Each family combines a story and a PMF
  • The Poisson as a limit of the binomial

Reading: Bernoulli’s Fallacy Ch. 3 (Quetelet)

Framing: FoAS deliberately avoids cataloging parametric families — that’s the “agnostic” stance. We add this unit because named distributions give us concrete objects for the expectation machinery from Session 2, and because χ², t, and F later in this session are the reference distributions of hypothesis testing.

Bernoulli

Bernoulli distribution

If \(X \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\), where \(0 \leq p \leq 1\), then \[ \Pr[X = x] = p^x (1-p)^{1-x}, \qquad x \in \{0, 1\}. \]

  • One trial, binary outcome; \(X = 1\) = “success”
    • Obviously a valid PMF: \((1 - p) + p = 1\)
  • This is the biased coin example from Session 1 (Example 1.2.7), now with a fancy name

Random variables in python

Create random variables using scipy.stats. For example, create Bernoulli r.v. with \(p = 0.3\):

X = stats.bernoulli(0.3)

Consider two calculations:

X.mean(), X.var()
(0.3, 0.21)
samples = X.rvs(size=1000)
samples.mean(), samples.var()
(0.331, 0.22143899999999997)

Can also do things like:

X.expect(lambda x: x**2) - X.expect(lambda x: x)**2
0.21

Geometric

  • Story: independent trials; \(X\) counts trials until the first success

Geometric distribution

If \(X \sim \operatorname{Geometric}(p)\), where \(0 < p \leq 1\), then \[ \Pr[X = x] = p(1-p)^{x-1}, \qquad x \in \{1, 2, \ldots\}. \]

  • First \((x - 1)\) trials fail, then success on trial \(x\)
    • read the PMF right from the story
  • Countably infinite support

Is the geometric PMF valid?

The probabilities must sum to one.

\[ \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \Pr[X = k] = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (1-p)^{k-1} p = p \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} r^j, \] where \(r = 1 - p\) and \(j = k - 1\). Since \(|r| < 1\), the geometric series formula gives

\[ \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} r^j = \frac{1}{1-r} = \frac{1}{p}. \] Therefore, \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \Pr[X = k] = p \cdot \frac{1}{p} = 1\).

Simulating waits

For \(p=0.3\), each random number below \(0.3\) represents a success. Consider three simulated sequences (rows) of four trials (columns):

p = 0.3
draws = np.array([[0.72, 0.11, 0.64, 0.08],
                  [0.94, 0.81, 0.46, 0.27],
                  [0.13, 0.71, 0.42, 0.88]])
waits = draws < p
waits, waits.argmax(axis=1) + 1
(array([[False,  True, False,  True],
        [False, False, False,  True],
        [ True, False, False, False]]),
 array([2, 4, 1]))
  • argmax(axis=1) finds the first True in each row, using a zero-based index. Adding 1 converts it to the trial count: waits of 2, 4, and 1.
  • The simulation applies the same operation to 100,000 rows of random draws.

Note

The simulation below checks only the first 16 trials. If all 16 fail, argmax returns 0 and incorrectly records a wait of 1. This happens with probability \(0.7^{16}\approx0.0033\) per row.

Geometric, simulated

p = 0.3; n = 100_000
waits = np.argmax(rng.random((n, 16)) < p, axis=1) + 1
x = np.arange(1, 15)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.hist(waits, bins=x - 0.5, density=True, alpha=0.4, label='simulated')
ax.stem(x, stats.geom(p).pmf(x), label=f'Geometric({p}) PMF')
ax.set(xlabel='trials until first success', ylabel='probability')
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Geometric moments

Let \(q=1-p\). Since \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} kq^{k-1}=1/(1-q)^2\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \E[X] &=p\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} kq^{k-1} =\frac{p}{(1-q)^2} =\frac{1}{p},\\[4pt] \end{aligned} \]

Similarly can show \(\V(X) = (1-p)/p^2\).

Binomial

  • Story: number of successes in \(n\) independent Bernoulli trials

Binomial distribution

If \(X \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n, p)\), where \(n\) is a positive integer and \(0 \leq p \leq 1\), then \[ \Pr[X = x] = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n\}. \]

  • \(\binom{n}{x}\) counts the ways to choose \(x\) successes from \(n\) trials
  • Validity: use the Binomial Theorem with \(a = p\), \(b = 1 - p\)

Binomial, simulated

n, p = 10, 0.3
draws = (rng.random((100_000, n)) < p).sum(axis=1)

x = np.arange(n + 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.hist(draws, bins=np.arange(n + 2) - 0.5, density=True, alpha=0.4,
        label='simulated')
ax.stem(x, stats.binom(n, p).pmf(x), label='Bin(10, 0.3) PMF')
ax.set(xlabel='successes', ylabel='probability')
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Binomial moments

Write \(X\) as the sum of \(n\) success indicators, each with expectation \(p\):

\[ X = \sum_{i=1}^n I_i \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \E[X] = \sum_{i=1}^n \E[I_i] = np. \]

The algebra for the variance is a bit more involved, but the result is \[ \V(X) = np(1-p). \]

A limit of the binomial

Fix the expected count \(np = 5\) and let \(n \to \infty\):

\[ \operatorname{Bin}\left(10, \tfrac{1}{2}\right),\; \operatorname{Bin}\left(100, \tfrac{1}{20}\right),\; \operatorname{Bin}\left(1000, \tfrac{1}{200}\right),\; \ldots \]

What happens to the PMF?

  • Does it flatten out, blow up, or settle down to something?
  • Many trials, each with tiny success probability — what real-world settings fit that description?

The Poisson limit

Poisson distribution

If \(X \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\), where \(\lambda > 0\), then \[ \Pr[X = x] = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^x}{x!}, \qquad x \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}. \]

With \(p_n = \lambda / n\):

\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \binom{n}{x} p_n^x (1 - p_n)^{n-x} = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^x}{x!}. \]

  • Counts of rare events in a fixed interval of time or space
  • Validity: factor out \(e^{-\lambda}\) and use the fact that \(\sum_k \lambda^k / k! = e^{\lambda}\)

History: Poisson 1837; made famous by Bortkiewicz’s 1898 study of Prussian cavalry deaths by horse kick — the canonical “rare events” dataset. Also worth prefiguring: later in this session we do the other binomial limit (p fixed, n → ∞, standardize) and get the normal. Two limits, two destinations.

Poisson and horse kicks

The Poisson limit

λ, x = 5, np.arange(16)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
for n in (10, 30, 1000):
    ax.plot(x, stats.binom(n, λ / n).pmf(x), 'o--', alpha=0.6,
            label=f'Bin({n}, {λ}/{n})')
ax.plot(x, stats.poisson(λ).pmf(x), 'k.-', label='Poisson(5)')
ax.set(xlabel='x', ylabel='f(x)')
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Negative binomial

Negative binomial distribution

If \(X\) is the number of failures before the \(r\)-th success, where \(r\) is a positive integer and \(0 < p \leq 1\), then \[ \Pr[X = x] = \binom{x + r - 1}{x} p^r (1-p)^x, \qquad x \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}. \]

  • Story: keep running trials until the \(r\)-th success; count the failures
  • \(r = 1\) recovers the geometric (but counting failures)

The discrete family tree

Name PMF Support Story
Bernoulli \(p^x(1-p)^{1-x}\) \(\{0,1\}\) One binary trial
Geometric \(p(1-p)^{x-1}\) \(1,2,\ldots\) Trials until first success
Binomial \(\binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x}\) \(0,\ldots,n\) Successes in \(n\) trials
Neg. binomial \(\binom{x+r-1}{x}p^r(1-p)^x\) \(0,1,\ldots\) Failures before \(r\)-th success
Poisson \(e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x/x!\) \(0,1,\ldots\) Rare-event counts
  • Every family is just a repackaging of Bernoulli trials

Continuous and normal-derived distributions

Exponential

Exponential distribution

If \(X \sim \operatorname{Exponential}(\lambda)\), where \(\lambda > 0\), then the PDF is \[ f_X(x; \lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad x \in [0, \infty). \]

  • Continuous analogue of the geometric: time until the next event, rather than trials until the first success
  • Validity: \(\int_0^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda x} dx = \left. -e^{-\lambda x} \right|_0^\infty = 1\)

Explore the exponential PDF and CDF

\[ f_X(x; \lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad x \in [0, \infty). \]

Exponential waiting times, simulated

waits = rng.exponential(scale=1/0.5, size=100_000)   # lambda = 0.5

x = np.linspace(0, 12, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.hist(waits, bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.4, label='simulated')
ax.plot(x, stats.expon(scale=2).pdf(x), 'k', label='Exponential(0.5) PDF')
ax.set(xlabel='waiting time', ylabel='density')
ax.set(xlim=(0, 12))
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Another binomial limit

As \(n \to \infty\), what does the distribution of \(X_n\) look like?

  • Earlier: \(p\) shrinking with \(n\) (\(np\) fixed) gave the Poisson
  • Now we fix \(p\) — different limit, different destination

Binomial → Normal

Normal

Normal distribution

If \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), where \(\sigma^2 > 0\), then the PDF is \[ f_X(x; \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}. \]

  • \(\mu = 0\), \(\sigma^2 = 1\): the standard normal
  • Standard notation: \(\phi(x; \mu, \sigma^2)\) for the PDF and \(\Phi(x; \mu, \sigma^2)\) for the CDF
  • Arises when an outcome is the sum of many small, roughly independent effects

No elementary antiderivative — validity needs the Gaussian integral (double integrals + polar coordinates)

Quantiles

Quantile

For \(c \in (0, 1)\), the \(c\)th quantile of \(X\) is \[ Q_X(c) = \min\{x \in \mathbb{R} : F_X(x) \geq c\}. \] If \(F_X\) is continuous and strictly increasing, \(Q_X(c) = F_X^{-1}(c)\).

  • The CDF maps a value to a probability; the quantile maps a probability back to a value
  • The \(c\)th quantile is the \(100c\)th percentile; \(Q_X(0.5)\) is the median

The min handles CDFs with jumps (discrete) or flat stretches, where no exact inverse exists. It is attained because CDFs are right-continuous.

Standard normal quantiles

Write \(z_c\) for the \(c\)th quantile of \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), so \(\Phi(z_c) = c\).

\(c\) 0.90 0.95 0.975 0.995
\(z_c\) 1.282 1.645 1.960 2.576
  • Symmetry: \(z_{1-c} = -z_c\), so \(z_{0.025} = -1.96\)

Explore normal percentiles

A return quantile

Example — Monthly return

Suppose a portfolio’s monthly return is \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0.01, 0.05^2)\). Since \(\Pr[X \leq \mu + \sigma z_c] = \Pr[Z \leq z_c] = c\), \[ Q_X(0.05) = 0.01 + 0.05 \, z_{0.05} = 0.01 - 0.05 \times 1.645 \approx -0.072. \]

  • A 5% chance of losing more than 7.2% in a month: the 5% value at risk

Quantiles, computed

mu, sigma = 0.01, 0.05

# ppf ('percent point function') is SciPy's name for the quantile function
ppf = stats.norm.ppf(0.05, loc=mu, scale=sigma)

# The sample quantile of simulated returns
returns = rng.normal(mu, sigma, size=100_000)
quantile_5 = np.quantile(returns, 0.05)

print(f'Analytic 5th percentile:  {ppf:.4f}')
print(f'Simulated 5th percentile: {quantile_5:.4f}')
Analytic 5th percentile:  -0.0722
Simulated 5th percentile: -0.0719

The De Moivre–Laplace theorem

De Moivre–Laplace theorem

Let \(X_n \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n, p)\) with \(q = 1 - p\). Then \[ \Pr[X_n = k] \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{npq}}\, \phi\!\left(\frac{k - np}{\sqrt{npq}}; 0, 1\right), \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{X_n - np}{\sqrt{npq}} \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0, 1). \]

  • The normal is not an assumption — it is derived as the large-\(n\) limit of coin flipping
  • De Moivre (1733) for \(p = \frac{1}{2}\); Laplace generalized
  • This is the ancestor of the Central Limit Theorem

BF Ch. 3 connection: this is exactly the “error law” lineage Clayton traces — De Moivre’s approximation → Laplace → Gauss/least squares → Quetelet transplanting it onto social data. The math today is the seed of that whole story.

Sketch of the derivation (I)

Step 1 — look near the mean. With \(\mu = np\), \(\sigma^2 = npq\), write \(k = np + z\sqrt{npq}\) for fixed \(z\).

Step 2 — Stirling’s approximation. For large \(m\), \[ m! \sim \sqrt{2\pi m}\left(\frac{m}{e}\right)^m. \]

Applied to \(\binom{n}{k}\), this yields \[ \Pr[X_n = k] \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \sqrt{\frac{n}{k(n-k)}} \frac{n^n p^k q^{n-k}}{k^k (n-k)^{n-k}}. \]

  • Everything else is just bookkeeping using logs and Taylor expansions

Sketch of the derivation (II)

Step 3 — take logs. With \(d = z\sqrt{npq}\), so \(k = np + d\) and \(n - k = nq - d\), expand \(\log(1 \pm u) = \pm u - \frac{u^2}{2} + o(u^2)\) to find

\[ \log\left(\frac{n^n p^k q^{n-k}}{k^k (n-k)^{n-k}}\right) = -\frac{z^2}{2} + o(1). \]

Step 4 — the constant. Since \(k \sim np\) and \(n - k \sim nq\), \(\sqrt{\frac{n}{k(n-k)}} \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{npq}}\).

Step 5 — recognize the density. \[ \Pr[X_n = k] \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi npq}}\, e^{-z^2/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{npq}}\,\phi(z; 0, 1). \qquad \blacksquare \]

  • The \(e^{-z^2/2}\) comes from the quadratic term of a Taylor expansion — that’s “why” the normal has its shape

The limit

p = 0.3
z = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
for n in (5, 25, 50):
    k = np.arange(n + 1)
    zk = (k - n * p) / np.sqrt(n * p * (1 - p))
    ax.plot(zk, stats.binom(n, p).pmf(k) * np.sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)),
            'o', ms=3, alpha=0.6, label=f'n = {n}')
ax.plot(z, stats.norm().pdf(z), 'k:', label=r'$\phi(z; 0, 1)$')
ax.set(xlim=(-4, 4), xlabel='z', ylabel='scaled PMF')
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Other distributions derived from the normal

  • Many important distributions are derived from the normal distribution
  • The most important are the \(\chi^2\), \(t\), and \(F\) distributions, which are the reference distributions for hypothesis testing
  • Some others include the log-normal, and the Gamma and Beta distributions, which are frequently used in Bayesian statistics

The \(\chi^2\) distribution

\(\chi^2\) distribution

Let \(Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_\nu\) be independent standard normal random variables. Then \[ X = \sum_{i=1}^{\nu} Z_i^2 \sim \chi^2_\nu \] (chi-square with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom), supported on \([0, \infty)\).

Try to visualize the shape of this distribution. How would the shape change as \(\nu\) increases?

The \(\chi^2\) PDF and CDF

\[ f_{\chi^2}(x; \nu) = \frac{1}{2^{\nu/2}\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)} x^{\nu/2 - 1} e^{-x/2}, \qquad x > 0. \]

Aside: The gamma function

\[ \Gamma(x) = \int_0^\infty s^{x-1} e^{-s} ds, \qquad x \in \mathbb{C}, \Re(x) > 0. \]

It can be shown that for any positive integer \(n\), \[\Gamma(n) = (n-1)\Gamma(n-1) = (n-1)!\] Therefore, the gamma function extends the factorial function to real (and complex) numbers.

The gamma function

from scipy.special import gamma, factorial

plt.figure(figsize=(7,4))
x = np.linspace(0.05,5.1,200)
plt.plot(x, gamma(x), 'g--')
n = np.arange(6)
plt.plot(n, gamma(n), 'ko')
plt.xlabel('$x$', fontsize=18)
plt.ylabel(r'$\Gamma(x)$', fontsize=18)
plt.grid(ls=':')
plt.show()

Constructions, verified

Z = rng.standard_normal((100_000, 5))
chi2_sim = (Z ** 2).sum(axis=1)                  # chi-square, 5 df

x = np.linspace(0, 20, 300)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.hist(chi2_sim, bins=80, density=True, alpha=0.4, label='sum of 5 $Z_i^2$')
ax.plot(x, stats.chi2(5).pdf(x), 'k', label=r'$\chi^2_5$ PDF')
ax.set(xlabel='x', ylabel='density')
ax.set_xlim(0, 20)
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Built from the normal: \(t\) and \(F\)

Student’s \(t\) distribution

Let \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and \(U \sim \chi^2_\nu\), independent. Then \[ T = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{U / \nu}} \sim t_\nu. \]

\(F\) distribution

Let \(U_1 \sim \chi^2_{d_1}\) and \(U_2 \sim \chi^2_{d_2}\), independent. Then \[ F = \frac{U_1 / d_1}{U_2 / d_2} \sim F_{d_1, d_2}. \]

  • \(t\): a normal divided by an estimate of its scale — heavier tails; \(t_\nu \to \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) as \(\nu \to \infty\)
  • \(F\): a ratio comparing two variances

Explore the Student’s \(t\) PDF and CDF

\[ f_t(x; \nu) = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu + 1}{2}\right)} {\sqrt{\nu\pi}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)} \left(1 + \frac{x^2}{\nu}\right)^{-\frac{\nu + 1}{2}}, \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Explore the \(F\) PDF and CDF

\[ f_F(x; d_1, d_2) = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{d_1 + d_2}{2}\right)} {\Gamma\!\left(\frac{d_1}{2}\right)\Gamma\!\left(\frac{d_2}{2}\right)} \left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^{d_1/2} x^{d_1/2 - 1} \left(1 + \frac{d_1}{d_2}x\right)^{-\frac{d_1 + d_2}{2}}, \qquad x > 0. \]

Log-normal

Log-normal distribution

Let \(Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) and define \(X = \exp(Y)\). Then \(X\) is log-normal: positive, right-skewed, and \(\log X\) is normal.

  • The workhorse for positive, skewed quantities: prices, firm sizes, durations
  • Multiplicative version of the normal’s additive story: products of many small factors

Explore the log-normal PDF and CDF

\[ f_X(x; \mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{x\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\log x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \qquad x > 0. \]

Percentiles

Continuous and normal-derived distributions recap

  • Exponential: continuous waiting times, the geometric’s analogue
  • The normal is derived: standardized binomial → \(\phi(z; 0, 1)\) via Stirling (De Moivre–Laplace) — the CLT’s ancestor
  • \(\chi^2\) (sum of squared normals), \(t\) (normal over estimated scale), \(F\) (variance ratio): the reference distributions of hypothesis testing
  • Next session: random samples, sampling distributions, and inference
